description:
The single fixture inventory for contracts/auth/v1/jsonschema/principal.v1.schema.json, read by the Go, Python and TypeScript golden runners. ONE manifest, ONE fixture directory, three runners -- three copies of one corpus is the drift G-70 exists to catch, so a runner that maintains its own list is a review defect.

`accept` is a positive control corpus carrying equal weight to `reject`: a validator that is too strict passes every rejection test while breaking every real caller, and that failure is invisible to a suite asserting only rejections.

Every identifier is unmistakably synthetic per G-73 (fixed EXAMPLE bodies, zero-padded counters, no plausible entropy) and the corpus is swept by a scanner rather than trusted to care -- G-16 forbids a credential value in any golden fixture, and these repos are public.
format_assertion_note: Two different things, do not conflate them. (1) CROSS-LANGUAGE FLOOR: every constraint a reject fixture asserts must use a keyword all three validators enforce -- in practice `pattern`, never `format`, because github.com/google/jsonschema-go records `format` and ignores it during validation (its doc.go, "Deviations from the specification"). (2) DEFENCE IN DEPTH where available: the Python and TypeScript runners MUST still enable format assertion (Python: Draft202012Validator(format_checker=...), which needs rfc3339-validator installed or it silently registers no date-time checker; TypeScript: ajv-formats) and MUST FAIL rather than skip if they cannot -- a format check that silently checks nothing while exiting 0 is the defect this contract exists to prevent.
regex_dialect_note: Every `pattern` here stays inside the common subset of Go RE2, ECMA-262 and Python `re`. RE2 has no back-references and no lookaround, and `\d`/`\w`/`\s` are Unicode in Python and ASCII in the other two. Guarded by a test with positive and negative controls, not by review.

reject.why: ACP-ADR-07 decision 2, G-14 and TRD section 8's own rule ("Grants and entitlements are not identity claims"): entitlement is an input to a decision and never a claim in a credential. This fixture is the executable form of that rule.

TRD section 11 and G-14 forbid embedding a complete mutable permission set in a credential. The first draft of this schema carried `permissions` copied from the legacy envelope; this fixture is what stops it coming back.

TRD section 3 and G-23: platform-admin authority moves to a separate platform role/action namespace resolved against current state. A superuser bit in a principal is the mechanism being migrated away from, not a field to preserve.
ACP-ADR-05 decision 4 / G-27: an explicit action at the call site, never a broad role check as the final decision.
ACP-ADR-05 decision 1 / G-26: unknown denies. A class absent from both the Wave 0 frozen 30 and the documented Wave 1 additions is not a compatibility convenience.
G-27: a single-segment action is the `is_admin` shape, made unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged.
Scopes are colon-separated and actions are dotted, deliberately different shapes so the two vocabularies cannot be confused at a call site (G-5: authentication is not authorization).
actor_chain is REQUIRED and explicitly empty when absent, so a deserializer defaulting a missing array to nil cannot make 'absent' read as 'not delegated'.
ACP-ADR-03 bounds a delegated session at 15 minutes and G-52 requires it revocable and shorter than the base session; a delegation with no expiry is an unbounded one.
The taxonomy is the Wave 0 closed vocabulary; unknown denies.

`amr` values are the RFC 8176 subset this platform can produce. Federated sign-in is identified by the credential class and the upstream identity, not by an amr value -- and `saml` is not a registered amr name.
NIST SP 800-63B defines aal1-aal3. An unrecognised assurance must deny, not compare greater-than by string order.
Empty string is not null. Python treats "" as falsy where Go nil-checks a pointer, so a contract accepting "" would mean two different things in two runtimes.
G-31 requires an allow-cache key to bind grant revision. A principal missing it lets a consumer build a cache key that a grant bump cannot invalidate.
Revisions are monotonic and non-negative.

TRD section 8 rule 1 / G-20: the authorization subject is the stable principal id, not the user record id. Using a subject id where a principal id belongs is the confusion the two separate fields exist to prevent, so the prefix makes it detectable.
G-13 requires an exact audience to be pinned; an absent audience is the fail-open case, because an empty expected audience disables the check in at least one JWT library.
A relying party must reject an unrecognised contract version rather than parse optimistically. TRD section 21: breaking semantics require v2, and a v2 document is not a v1 document.

The enforced keyword is `pattern`, not `format`: github.com/google/jsonschema-go records `format` and ignores it during validation, so a fixture asserting `format` would be checked in Python and TypeScript and vacuous in Go.
Same cross-language floor as expires_at, asserted on a NESTED field -- a walker or a validator that only enforced the top level would pass this.

REGRESSION GUARD for a MEASURED divergence. With the digit class spelled \d this exact document was ACCEPTED by the Python validator and REJECTED by the Go one: Python's `re` treats \d as Unicode and matches Devanagari digits, Go RE2 and ECMA-262 treat it as ASCII. Every digit class is now [0-9], and this fixture is what stops \d being reintroduced -- under \d it turns green in one language and stays red in another.
